compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In the same discussion, two people might both ask what evidence supports a proposal and remain open to an alternative. Shared T and P can help explain those preferences. The discussion itself cannot tell you which type either person is.

T and P address different questions. Thinking concerns the criteria for choosing. Perceiving concerns keeping options open to new information. Neither measures warmth or how quickly someone makes a decision.

E/I addresses where attention and energy tend to go. S/N addresses what information carries weight. Someone can reflect privately on a set of measurements or discuss possible explanations with a group. The two pairs describe separate aspects of preference.

### ESTP and INTP: an unfamiliar fault, and the first information each reaches for

In this fictional example, an office air conditioner stops cooling. Two staff members have the same report and neither is assigned to repair it. The report says it worked yesterday, began blowing warm air this morning, and shows no error message.

Both staff members can review the same fault log and maintenance history. One way to read them is to identify verified changes and when they occurred. Another is to compare reports across operating conditions and identify possible patterns. Qualified personnel handle inspection and repair.

An INTP can notice a concrete change and an ESTP can look for a recurring pattern. Training and authority determine who can inspect equipment. The order in which someone reads the records does not identify a type.

compare_blocks.body:
The two scenarios below are fictional. They illustrate how people learn and share information. Driving practice remains under the instructor’s supervision, and clinical decisions belong to qualified professionals.

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In the same discussion, two people might both ask what evidence supports a proposal and remain open to an alternative. Shared T and P can help explain those preferences. The discussion itself cannot tell you which type either person is.

T and P address different questions. Thinking concerns the criteria for choosing. Perceiving concerns keeping options open to new information. Neither measures warmth or how quickly someone makes a decision.

E/I addresses where attention and energy tend to go. S/N addresses what information carries weight. Someone can reflect privately on a set of measurements or discuss possible explanations with a group. The two pairs describe separate aspects of preference.

### ESTP and INTP: an unfamiliar fault, and the first information each reaches for

In this fictional example, an office air conditioner stops cooling. Two staff members have the same report and neither is assigned to repair it. The report says it worked yesterday, began blowing warm air this morning, and shows no error message.

Both staff members can review the same fault log and maintenance history. One way to read them is to identify verified changes and when they occurred. Another is to compare reports across operating conditions and identify possible patterns. Qualified personnel handle inspection and repair.

A fault log cannot capture everything, and a pattern across a few reports can have several explanations. Combine specific observations and possible explanations when deciding what information to pass on.

An INTP can notice a concrete change and an ESTP can look for a recurring pattern. Training and authority determine who can inspect equipment. The order in which someone reads the records does not identify a type.

For reflection, record what evidence you noticed, what connection you considered, and what information would change your view. Compare similar low-risk situations where you had a choice. The notes do not determine your type.

### ESTP and INTP: both list Ti and Fe, yet the perceiving side differs

In type dynamics, P points to an outward-facing perceiving process. For the extraverted ESTP, that process is dominant extraverted Sensing (Se), supported by introverted Thinking (Ti). For the introverted INTP, it is auxiliary extraverted Intuition (Ne), supporting dominant Ti.

In the notation used here, ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni and INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe. Both use Ti in the model to check internal consistency, but it pairs with Se for ESTP and Ne for INTP. Either person can check a specific observation or test whether a proposed explanation fits multiple observations.

Extraverted Feeling (Fe) is tertiary for ESTP in this notation and inferior for INTP. The position describes a role in the model and does not measure social skills or consideration for others.

The Foundation lists tertiary Feeling for ESTP (Fe or Fi) and tertiary Sensing for INTP (Se or Si). This page uses Fe and Si. The alternatives leave the dominant and auxiliary processes unchanged. Read the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp) for more detail.

compare_blocks.body:
The two scenarios below are fictional. They illustrate how people learn and share information. Driving practice remains under the instructor’s supervision, and clinical decisions belong to qualified professionals.

In this fictional lesson, two learners have the same instructor, car, practice time, and feedback. Either can ask the instructor to explain the maneuver or discuss what happened during supervised practice.

ESTP and INTP place Ti in different positions and have different perceiving processes in the model: Se and Ni for ESTP, Ne and Si for INTP. The model describes which kinds of information may get more weight. It cannot tell you what conclusion either person will reach from the same evidence.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In the same discussion, two people might both ask what evidence supports a proposal and remain open to an alternative. Shared T and P can help explain those preferences. The discussion itself cannot tell you which type either person is.

T and P address different questions. Thinking concerns the criteria for choosing. Perceiving concerns keeping options open to new information. Neither measures warmth or how quickly someone makes a decision.

E/I addresses where attention and energy tend to go. S/N addresses what information carries weight. Someone can reflect privately on a set of measurements or discuss possible explanations with a group. The two pairs describe separate aspects of preference.

### ESTP and INTP: an unfamiliar fault, and the first information each reaches for

In this fictional example, an office air conditioner stops cooling. Two staff members have the same report and neither is assigned to repair it. The report says it worked yesterday, began blowing warm air this morning, and shows no error message.

Both staff members can review the same fault log and maintenance history. One way to read them is to identify verified changes and when they occurred. Another is to compare reports across operating conditions and identify possible patterns. Qualified personnel handle inspection and repair.

A fault log cannot capture everything, and a pattern across a few reports can have several explanations. Combine specific observations and possible explanations when deciding what information to pass on.

An INTP can notice a concrete change and an ESTP can look for a recurring pattern. Training and authority determine who can inspect equipment. The order in which someone reads the records does not identify a type.

For reflection, record what evidence you noticed, what connection you considered, and what information would change your view. Compare similar low-risk situations where you had a choice. The notes do not determine your type.

### ESTP and INTP: both list Ti and Fe, yet the perceiving side differs

In type dynamics, P points to an outward-facing perceiving process. For the extraverted ESTP, that process is dominant extraverted Sensing (Se), supported by introverted Thinking (Ti). For the introverted INTP, it is auxiliary extraverted Intuition (Ne), supporting dominant Ti.

In the notation used here, ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni and INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe. Both use Ti in the model to check internal consistency, but it pairs with Se for ESTP and Ne for INTP. Either person can check a specific observation or test whether a proposed explanation fits multiple observations.

Extraverted Feeling (Fe) is tertiary for ESTP in this notation and inferior for INTP. The position describes a role in the model and does not measure social skills or consideration for others.

The Foundation lists tertiary Feeling for ESTP (Fe or Fi) and tertiary Sensing for INTP (Se or Si). This page uses Fe and Si. The alternatives leave the dominant and auxiliary processes unchanged. Read the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp) for more detail.

sections.body_md:
Read each example with the same task, information, deadline, and authority on both sides. Either person could use both approaches. The third and fourth rows illustrate shared preferences.

| Same task and information | ESTP: possible emphasis | INTP: possible emphasis | What the row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Reviewing the same fault report | Which details the report actually confirms | Which connections across the same entries could explain the fault | S/N: documented details and possible patterns. Qualified personnel inspect equipment. |
| Discussing the same unresolved question | Attention may turn outward toward the exchange with colleagues | Attention may turn inward toward reflection on the same question | E/I: orientation of attention and energy. Either can talk or reflect. |
| Reviewing an existing process | Apply the same criterion to what the records show about the current method | Apply the same criterion to whether the explanation for the method still fits | Shared T: either can decide against the same consistently applied criterion |
| A plan changes halfway through | Keep room to adjust the arrangements as confirmed conditions change | Keep room to adjust the arrangements if an assumption proves wrong | Shared P: either can keep workable options open |
| Learning in the same supervised session | Notice specific steps and feedback from the instructor | Look for a pattern in that same feedback that may apply to another task | S/N: details and possible connections. Both can use the feedback. |
| Reviewing the same event later | What the notes confirm about what happened and under what conditions | What recurring connections across the notes suggest about why it happened | S/N: recorded details and possible explanations, with no claim about memory ability |
| Working with unfamiliar colleagues | Attention may turn outward to the interaction as the group makes sense of the task | Attention may turn inward to working through the same information privately | E/I: either person can contribute to the discussion. Speaking order does not identify the preference. |

A person with experience may know which record to check. A newcomer may need to ask for background. Responsibilities and available information can explain those choices. This table does not measure competence or validate a type result.
sections.title: ESTP and INTP in one minute

sections.body_md:
The two scenarios below are fictional. They illustrate how people learn and share information. Driving practice remains under the instructor’s supervision, and clinical decisions belong to qualified professionals.

### ESTP and INTP: learning a manoeuvre, and what feel and theory each cost

In this fictional lesson, two learners have the same instructor, car, practice time, and feedback. Either can ask the instructor to explain the maneuver or discuss what happened during supervised practice.

One way to learn from the session is to record where the car was and what feedback the instructor gave. Another is to ask how those observations relate to one another and which parts of the explanation might carry over to a different car.

A familiar reference point can help during practice and still need checking in a different car. Understanding the relationship does not replace supervised practice. The instructor helps each learner decide which questions to work on.

An INTP can learn from direct feedback, and an ESTP can ask for a diagram. Both approaches can help the same person and neither identifies type.

To reflect on learning, note what you observed, which explanation helped, and whether the conditions mattered. These notes can guide questions for the instructor and cannot determine type.

### ESTP and INTP: dividing a routine follow-up appointment

In this fictional follow-up visit, two relatives accompany a family member to a scheduled appointment. Both have permission to help and access to the same records.

One task is keeping track of check-in and the documents requested by the clinic. Another is helping the family member organize the information they want to share, such as previous results, observed changes, and questions for the clinician.

If no one checks the appointment instructions, the family may arrive without a requested document. If no one looks through the records, a question the family member wanted to ask may be forgotten. Both tasks serve the same visit.

The family member’s wishes, familiarity with the clinic, and access to the records guide who helps with each task. Either relative can do both.

The clinician decides what assessment or tests are needed. Relatives can help describe observed changes and share information with the family member’s permission. What someone does at the appointment cannot identify their type or show how much they care.

An ESTP can spend time alone, and an INTP can enjoy a long discussion. E/I concerns the direction of attention and energy. Sociability and speaking time cannot establish it.

An INTP can be precise about measurements, and an ESTP can consider several possible explanations. S/N concerns the kinds of information that get more weight. It does not measure practicality.

Ti refers to checking internal consistency in the model. Tone depends on the wording and the situation. Either type can raise a logical concern considerately.

Ti and Fe occupy different positions in the notation used here. The perceiving processes also differ. The model cannot predict how well two people work together or who should lead.

Training, responsibility, time, and available information can determine who speaks or acts first. Do not use that order to identify ESTP or INTP.

sections.body_md:
If results disagree, compare the instrument, version, language, and scoring guidance. Consider what situations you had in mind. Job demands can shape the examples you recall without establishing that a preference changed.

Recall several ordinary decisions where you had similar responsibilities and a real choice. Note what information you used, what connections you considered, and whether discussion or private reflection helped you make sense of it. The exercise is for reflection and cannot determine your type.

Include cases where you did something different. They show how circumstances can change what is useful or what feels natural.
